title: Supreme Court strikes down UP laws that denied pensions to regularised work-charged staff
dek: The court said Uttar Pradesh could not use new laws to undo its 2019 ruling, and ordered pension claims of retired employees to be settled within six months or carry 9% interest.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Supreme Court has struck down two Uttar Pradesh laws that excluded years spent in work-charged, temporary and daily-wage jobs from the service counted for government pensions, holding that the state could not use fresh legislation to undo a binding 2019 ruling of the court.

In a judgment dated 18 November, a bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma declared the Uttar Pradesh Qualifying Service for Pension and Validation Act, 2021 and the Uttar Pradesh Entitlement to Pension and Validation Act, 2025 unconstitutional. Retired employees whose jobs were later regularised can now claim pensions that count their earlier service, and the state must decide each claim within six months, the court ordered.

## What the laws did

In Prem Singh v State of Uttar Pradesh in 2019, the Supreme Court held that service in work-charged posts, staff paid from the budget of a particular work or project rather than against a sanctioned post, must count as qualifying service for pension once the employee is regularised. It read down a rule of the state's 1961 retirement benefits rules that had excluded it.

The 2021 Act redefined "qualifying service" to mean service against a temporary or permanent post under the service rules, and retrospectively validated pension denials going back to 1 April 1961. The 2025 Act introduced the term "substantive appointee", limited pensions to such employees, excluded some who had subscribed to provident funds, and again validated past denials.

## What the court said

The bench held that once an employee is regularised under a properly framed scheme, the nature of the first appointment cannot be used to deny pension. "The act of regularisation obliterates the source or birthmark of the appointment simpliciter," the judgment says.

A legislature may pass a law to overcome a court ruling, but only by removing the defect the court identified. The test, the court said, is "whether it has removed the infirmity which rendered the exclusion constitutionally unsustainable". It found that both Acts kept the same exclusion under new labels. "The existence of a new definition does not, by itself, establish that the defect" had been cured, it said.

## What changes for employees

The court directed that:

- retired employees covered by the judgment may file pension claims with full service details with the competent authority, which must decide them within six months and release what is due
- arrears are limited to three years before the Prem Singh petition was filed, except for claims by the heirs of employees who retired and died before that ruling, who must provide "unimpeachable proof"
- a claim cannot be rejected without a hearing and a reasoned order, and an employee whose claim is allowed must be given a chart of every payment
- the state will not pay interest for the period the invalid laws were in force, but if it misses the deadlines it must pay simple interest at 9 per cent a year until payment

The judgment also gives the state a final six months to comply with Prem Singh in pending contempt cases, and warns that further non-compliance may be treated as aggravated contempt. It sets aside the Allahabad High Court orders the employees had appealed against.

The judgment, as reported, does not say how many employees are affected. The lead petitioner was an association of non-gazetted employees of the state's ground water department.

## What happens next

The Uttar Pradesh government had not said publicly by Sunday whether it would seek a review. Retired employees can begin filing claims with their departments, and the six-month clock for each claim runs from the date it is received.
